papers.title: Stream and lake network position structures freshwater microbial communities across multiple catchments
papers.abstract: Streams and lakes form hydrologically connected freshwater networks. Different environmental conditions and dispersal dynamics along the stream to lake continuum potentially affect bacterial community composition, although the strength of such effects may vary among individual catchments. Here, we analysed 224 water samples from 58 streams draining into eight lakes across Switzerland, covering the full continuum from headwaters to lake outlets. Bacterial community composition analyzed via 16S metabarcoding differed between streams and lakes, with a sharp turnover at stream and lake confluence, and this pattern was repeatable across all catchments. Lake communities had lower alpha diversity and lower overall beta dispersion than stream communities, despite hydrological connectivity with a diverse stream microbiome. Community composition in both lakes and streams differed between catchments, but this pattern was more pronounced in lakes. Lake communities were dominated by a small set of widespread and abundant core taxa, primarily established pelagic freshwater genera, that captured the catchment-level differences through shifts in relative abundance. In contrast, stream communities contained a comparatively less abundant core microbiome dominated by soil- and groundwater-associated genera, together with a larger and more diverse peripheral microbiome. Together, these findings show that bacterial community composition changes repeatably across the different positions of hydrological networks.

papers.title: CyranoPS, a novel compact temperate corynephage infecting Corynebacterium glutamicum MB001
papers.abstract: Here, we describe CyranoPS, a temperate phage isolated from the river Yvette in France, using the prophage-free strain Corynebacterium glutamicum MB001. Negative-stain electron microscopy revealed virions with siphovirus morphology. Its 14,910-bp genome has a GC content of 53.0% and 14-nt 3' overhangs at both ends. It carries 26 predicted genes, 10 without predicted functions, and no tRNAs. CyranoPS belongs to the newly established actinophage cluster ER, whose members have the smallest known genomes among Corynebacterium-infecting phages. Deletion of genes encoding the porin PorAH and the protein mycoloyltransferase MytC abolished infection, while genes encoding the mycomembrane proteins PorBC and ProtX were dispensable. CyranoPS established lysogeny in C. glutamicum through chromosomal integration probably mediated by its predicted tyrosine integrase. Integration truncated the immunity repressor gene Cyr_18, resulting in a protein devoid of its 15 C-terminal residues. The truncated repressor conferred stronger protection against superinfection than the full-length repressor. CyranoPS lysogens exhibited high levels of spontaneous prophage induction, reaching 109 PFU/mL under standard conditions, with no further increase upon treatment with mitomycin C. These findings suggest a potentially SOS-independent lytic-lysogenic switch and establish CyranoPS as a compact model to study infection and lysogeny regulation in Mycobacteriales.

papers.title: More insights into the dynamic assembly and rotation of the archaellum motor machinery
papers.abstract: Archaea use the archaellum for swimming motility. Rotation of the archaellum is driven by the ATPase ArlI and the membrane platform protein ArlJ. Structural studies suggest that conformational changes in ArlI power the rotation of ArlJ. However, how ATP hydrolysis is converted into rotation remains poorly under-stood. Using single-molecule total internal reflection fluorescence (TIRF) microscopy, we show that dimeric ArlJ forms a complex with ArlI. Combining conservation analysis, AlphaFold3 predictions and co-purifications, we identified conserved ArlJ residues required for interaction with ArlI, including a structural-ly rigid loop and the critical residue R341 at the ArlI interface. Motility assays in Haloferax volcanii confirmed these findings. Together, these findings support a model in which a dimeric ArlJ is interacting with ArlI via conserved residues to generate torque.

papers.title: Mobile genetic elements accompany the emergence of clonal crop lineages from weed-associated populations of Xanthomonas campestris
papers.abstract: Xanthomonas campestris is a destructive pathogen of cruciferous vegetables and ornamentals and is frequently isolated from related weed species growing near agricultural land. However, the evolutionary relationships, genomic features, and biosecurity significance of weed-associated strains remain poorly understood. Here, we integrate phylogenomic and pangenomic analyses of X. campestris, including nine newly sequenced strains isolated from invasive garlic mustard (Alliaria petiolata), to compare strains from cultivated and non-cultivated hosts across multiple pathovars. Weed-isolated strains predominantly clustered within basal, genetically diverse lineages associated with broad host ranges, whereas crop-isolated strains were concentrated in host-associated clonal lineages. The emergence of specialized crop-associated lineages coincided with multiple inferred acquisitions of large mobile elements, including integrative conjugative and mobilizable elements and plasmids carrying genes previously associated with pathogenicity and host range. Although these elements were enriched in clonal crop-associated lineages, they also occurred in diverse weed-associated strains, indicating that genetic material associated with crop infection is distributed among divergent lineages and persists in wild and weedy systems. These findings identify invasive weeds as ancillary hosts that may harbor pathogen diversity and provide opportunities for genetic exchange, underscoring the importance of surveillance beyond agricultural fields to monitor pathogen diversification and emerging threats. Our pangenomic analysis also identified crop-associated pathogen factors and putative host resistance targets for future investigation, providing a foundation for developing critically needed black rot-resistant cultivars.

papers.title: oidyPeaks: R package for automated flow cytometry cell cycle analysis and visualization in fungal microbes
papers.abstract: Karyotypic variation in fungal populations from ecological, clinical, and industrial environments and is also a hallmark of many cancers. The evolutionary dynamics of karyotypic vriants (i.e., changes in the number of chromosomes, either as complete sets or single chromosomes) are the same as any de novo mutation. To quantify karyotypic subpopulations within evolving populations, an unbiased computational method is required to identify subpopulations and quantify their abundance. Flow cytometry is the standard method to measure the genome size from large populations of individual cells. Cell populations typically include cells in all stages of the cell cycle (G0/G1 before DNA replication, S phase during replication, and G2/M after DNA replication but before cell division). Existing mathematical models can be fit to genome-size distributions to determine the base ploidy of a population, but existing algorithms assume a single base ploidy. Mixed-karyotype populations therefore require manual gating to subdivide the flow cytometry data before analysis, which introduces bias, as it is not always clear where or when gates should be drawn. To overcome this, we developed a new method that identifies and quantifies karyotypic subpopulations from flow cytometry data. The open-source R package ploidyPeaks builds on existing Bioconductor tools to import and manipulate standard .fcs flow cytometry files. Using reference populations of known ploidy, we established thresholds to distinguish single-genome size populations and identify candidate mixed-karyotype samples. We then developed a peak-detection algorithm to identify G0/G1 and G2/M peaks, resolve karyotypic subpopulations within mixed populations, and apply nonlinear least-squares fitting of the Dean-Jett-Fox cell-cycle model to each subpopulation, providing a confidence measure for model fit. Compared with existing methods, our approach quantifies genome size in mixed-karyotype populations without manual intervention while providing an objective measure of model fit. We demonstrate the utility of this method on 240 replicate populations initiated from 20 Candida albicans genetic backgrounds evolving for 100 generations to the antifungal drug fluconazole.

papers.title: Enhanced Antimicrobial Potency and Therapeutic Index of a Defined C12 Quaternary Ammonium Compound
papers.abstract: Skin and soft tissue infections (SSTIs) remain a major clinical burden and are complicated by antimicrobial resistance, polymicrobial infections, and biofilm-mediated therapeutic tolerance. Topical antimicrobials can provide localized activity while reducing systemic exposure, but currently available agents are limited by narrow spectra, cytotoxicity, poor antibiofilm activity, and resistance development. We evaluated C12-alkyl(ethylbenzyl)dimethyl ammonium chloride (EQ12), a next-generation quaternary ammonium compound, in vitro as a topical antimicrobial candidate for leading bacterial causes of SSTIs. Broth microdilution assays were used to determine minimum inhibitory concentrations (MICs) and minimum bactericidal concentrations (MBCs) against methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA), methicillin-resistant S. aureus (MRSA), Acinetobacter baumannii, Klebsiella pneumoniae, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Species-selective plating was used to assess bactericidal activity in staphylococcal-P. aeruginosa co-cultures. Crystal violet assays quantified biofilm inhibition against MRSA, P. aeruginosa, and A. baumannii, and serial passage experiments assessed resistance emergence over 14 passages. EQ12 inhibited all species tested, with MICs of 2.3 to 40 micrograms/mL and MBCs of 4.7 to 40 micrograms/mL. EQ12 outperformed benzalkonium chloride and povidone-iodine against Gram-negative isolates and retained bactericidal activity in mixed cultures, although staphylococcal susceptibility decreased in the presence of P. aeruginosa. EQ12 inhibited biofilm formation at sub-MIC to near-MIC concentrations and did not induce resistance in MRSA, P. aeruginosa, or A. baumannii, unlike comparator topical antibiotics. These findings support further development of EQ12 as a topical antimicrobial for SSTI-associated pathogens.

papers.title: A bacterial chaperone-usher pathway links interkingdom association to antimicrobial protection of a fungal partner
papers.abstract: Antimicrobial compounds (AMCs) influence species-level composition of microbial communities, governing beneficial and pathogenic interactions with plant and mammalian hosts. Phenazine-1-carboxylic acid (PCA) is a bacterially produced, redox-active AMC abundant in the rhizosphere. A recent study discovered the PCA-susceptible fungus Aspergillus calidoustus can grow in PCA-abundant environments by associating with phenazine-tolerant bacteria, including the novel species Paraburkholderia edwinii. P. edwinii's protection response is characterized by adherence to its fungal partner, bacterial aggregation, and sequestration and reduction of PCA, rendering PCA less toxic. Deletion of the bacterial transcriptional repressor HrcA generates a constitutively active protection response and enhanced protection of A. calidoustus. Here, we use the {Delta}hrcA strain to determine whether fungal protection uses bacterial self-protection machinery or dedicated interkingdom mechanisms. We identified a divergent archaic chaperone-usher pathway (CUP) operon encoding a predicted periplasmic chaperone, outer membrane usher, putative major pilin-like subunit, and putative adhesin-like tip protein. While many archaic CUP operons are annotated in diverse bacteria, their functions remain largely unexplored. We show these fungal attachment complex ( fac ) genes promote bacterial-fungal attachment, are required for P. edwinii to sequester and detoxify PCA, and contribute to full fungal protection from PCA stress, despite not being required for P. edwinii's own tolerance of PCA. We further identified the transcription regulator, FacR, that influences expression of the fac system. Understanding the functions of divergent archaic CUP systems may illuminate protective interkingdom partnerships and inform how pathogenic and beneficial microbes gain entry to AMC-replete environments, shaping microbial communities in agricultural and clinical contexts.

papers.title: Molecular characterization of thermo-adapted Novirhabdovirus variants and virulence in vivo in rainbow trout and zebrafish at different temperatures.
papers.abstract: Controlling viral diseases in fish is a challenge for the sustainable development of aquaculture and improving the health of fish farms. Infectious hematopoietic necrosis virus (IHNV) is a major pathogen in aquaculture. It infects cold-water fish, but loses its infectivity at temperatures above 20{degrees}C. Since fish are poikilothermic animals, their body temperature fluctuates according to that of their environment. Faced with current climate change, it is crucial to understand how these pathogens will adapt to rising temperatures. Through a strategy simulating the impact of global warming, this virus has been progressively thermo-adapted to 25{degrees}C. The selected variant, IHNV25, replicates at 25{degrees}C while maintaining efficient replication at low temperatures, like its parental strain. Genome sequencing and a reverse genetics approach revealed that only 9 amino acid substitutions, distributed across 4 of the 6 viral genes, were essential for thermo-adaptation. Although IHNV25 was highly attenuated in its natural host, the rainbow trout, at any temperatures, it proved highly virulent when injected in zebrafish larvae at 20{degrees}C and 25{degrees}C, inducing severe symptoms identical to those observed in trout (hemorrhages, oedema, and exophthalmia). At both temperatures, mortality was preceded by a massive viral replication and a delayed and inefficient interferon and inflammatory response. Unlike the parental strain, IHNV25 was also capable of infecting larvae by bath immersion at 25{degrees}C, entering via the caudal fin, thus demonstrating its ability to cross the species barrier. The identification of viral markers of thermo-adaptation will therefore be of great interest for the epidemiological surveillance of field isolates.

papers.title: Structure-activity relationship study in soil identifies an effective broad-spectrum inhibitor of archaeal nitrification
papers.abstract: Ammonia-oxidizing archaea (AOA) can contribute substantially to nitrification in agricultural soils, yet the portfolio of AOA-targeting nitrification inhibitors (NIs) with demonstrated efficacy under soil conditions remains limited. Moreover, the performance of candidate inhibitors in soil is often difficult to predict from pure-culture assays because their activity is strongly influenced by soil-dependent factors. In this study, we employed a recently developed high-throughput miniaturized soil incubation assay to perform a soil-based structure-activity relationship (SAR) analysis of SIAS (Specific Inhibitor of AOA in Soil), a pyrazolo-pyridine derivative previously identified as an AOA-targeting compound with strong additive nitrification inhibition effects when combined with the AOB-targeting inhibitor DMP (3,4-dimethyl-1H-pyrazole). To identify structural features associated with improved and more robust soil efficacy, a library of 27 SIAS-derived pyrazolo-pyridine analogues was evaluated directly in soil. The SAR analysis showed that inhibitory activity was governed by a specific combination of structural features and led to the discovery of Optimized SIAS (Opt. SIAS), a simplified analogue that consistently outperformed the original lead compound across diverse agricultural soils. Correlation analysis further revealed that soil pH and, particularly, silt content were major determinants of Opt. SIAS efficacy. The strong additive effects obtained through combined application of Opt. SIAS and DMP highlight the contribution of AOA to residual nitrification following AOB inhibition and demonstrate the potential of simultaneously targeting both groups. Together, these results expand the limited portfolio of effective AOA-targeting nitrification inhibitors and provide a foundation for the development of next-generation nitrification inhibition strategies aimed at improving nitrogen-use efficiency and reducing nitrogen losses from agricultural soils.

papers.title: CpxR-CpxS two-component system exacerbates development of antibiotic resistance in Pseudomonas aeruginosa
papers.abstract: Pseudomonas aeruginosa, as a member of the ESKAPE pathogens, is well known for its ability to develop multidrug resistance following antibiotic therapy. Overexpression of the efflux pumps, often caused by dysfunction of related transcriptional factors, is well known as a common mechanism underpins multidrug resistance. Previous work showed direct regulatory link of CpxR-CpxS, an OmpR-EnvZ family two-component system, with the expression of the predominant MexAB-OprM efflux pump in P. aeruginosa. However, the contribution of this regulatory link to the development of antibiotic resistance has not been fully elucidated. In this work, it has been shown that deletion of cpxR, but not cpxS, reduces the emergence of multidrug resistant colonies almost 1000 times lower compared to the parental wild type P. aeruginosa PA14 following sub-lethal antibiotic exposure, suggesting that apart from CpxS, other sensory component(s) or pathway(s) can also mediate CpxR activity in the development of antibiotic resistance in P. aeruginosa. We further demonstrate that when glucose is used as the sole carbon source, it leads to increased expression levels of mexA and reduced antibiotics susceptibilities in the PA14{Delta}cpxS strain in a cpxR dependent manner. GtrS, another EnvZ family sensor kinase, but not the well-known AckA-Pta pathway, mediates this glucose effects. Both in vivo and in vitro evidences support that GtrS can activate CpxR in a cross-talk manner in the absence of CpxS. Besides gtrS, at least four other sensor kinase genes (envZ, tctE, phoR and colS) can exert activation effect upon CpxR in the PA14{Delta}cpxS strain. Having the risk of multiple way to antibiotic resistance development, cpxS null mutations can be emerged in P. aeruginosa clinical isolates. Since many OmpR-EnvZ family two-component system have been shown to be engaged in antibiotic resistance, its potential risk of exacerbating antibiotic resistance in ESKAPE pathogens has been discussed.

papers.title: A broadly active flavivirus NS4B targeting compound that blocks NS4B-NS3 binding and replication organelle formation
papers.abstract: Mosquito-borne orthoflaviviruses, including West Nile virus (WNV), dengue virus (DENV), Zika virus (ZIKV), and Japanese encephalitis virus (JEV), cause substantial global morbidity and mortality, yet no broadly effective direct-acting antivirals are available. The viral nonstructural protein NS4B has emerged as a promising antiviral target, although the compounds described to date are largely DENV-specific. Here we characterize SRI-38841, a xanthine analog derived from hit-to-lead optimization of a previously described WNV inhibitor, which inhibits WNV replication with an IC90 of 0.87 {micro}M and low cytotoxicity, and retains activity against DENV, ZIKV, and JEV. Serial passage of WNV under compound selection yielded resistant viruses bearing mutations in NS4B, and reverse genetics was used to confirm the role of individual amino acid substitutions. Several of these residues map to regions analogous to those implicated in resistance to the DENV NS4B inhibitors JNJ-A07 and NITD-688. Docking of SRI-38841 to an AlphaFold2 model of WNV NS4B predicted a binding pocket within a cytosolic-facing funnel, and mutation of the pocket residues A45 and K56 likewise conferred resistance, while changes at Q170 and T220 did not. Together, these data favor a topology model in which the compound engages a cytosolic-facing pocket over one placing these residues in the ER lumen. Mechanistically, SRI-38841 disrupts the NS4B-NS3 interaction and abolishes replication organelle formation in infected cells. Unlike JNJ-A07 and NITD-688, which were inactive against WNV and ZIKV, SRI-38841 inhibits all four viruses tested, identifying this xanthine class as a starting point for broadly active orthoflavivirus antivirals.

papers.title: Iron as a critical determinant for survival, oxidative stress, and infectivity of Leishmania parasites
papers.abstract: Iron is an essential for all living organisms, including humans, and is present in RBCs & other iron-binding proteins that play crucial roles in oxygen transport, DNA synthesis & electron transport. Similarly, iron also plays a critical role in parasite biology. The unicellular Leishmania parasites scavenge essential iron inside host macrophages. We investigated the impact of iron on parasite growth, apoptosis, oxidative stress, and the expression of proteins involved in ROS, thiol metabolism, Fe-S clusters, and infectivity in macrophages. Our findings revealed that optimum iron concentrations promote parasite proliferation, whereas higher levels induce toxicity, leading to DNA fragmentation and caspase-like activity. Iron supplementation enhances parasite tolerance to oxidative stress by decreasing intracellular ROS and increasing total intracellular thiol content in a concentration-dependent manner. However, iron depletion increases ROS levels and decreases total thiol content in a concentration-dependent manner, which disrupts redox homeostasis. To support our finding, we further exposed these treated parasites to menadione, which supports that iron-supplemented cells can better survive under oxidative stress than the depleted cells. Furthermore, extra iron availability increases the expression of key metabolic proteins, Fe-S clusters (Nbp35, Frataxin, IScU) and thiol metabolism (TryS, TryR, CS, SAT, cTXN, cTXNPx), while under iron-depleted conditions these proteins were downregulated except frataxin. In vitro infectivity demonstrated that iron supplementation enhances parasite infectivity, while iron depletion impairs percentage infectivity. Our study demonstrates the roles of iron in the survival, redox regulation, and virulence of L. donovani, which can correlate with the role of cellular iron homeostasis in VL pathogenesis.

papers.title: Phosphatidylserine receptors are critical for lethal infection by Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever virus
papers.abstract: The tick-borne Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever virus (CCHFV) causes severe and often fatal hemorrhagic disease for which no approved countermeasures are available. Herein, we identify the phosphatidylserine receptors (PSRs) AXL, TIM-1, and TIM-4 as critical entry host factors for CCHFV in cell lines and liver-derived primary cell cultures. Small-molecule and antibody-based PSR inhibitors greatly reduced viral infection in cell culture. Germline knockout of individual PSR genes afforded partial protection against CCHFV infection, disease, and death in a murine model of lethal viral challenge. Mice engineered to lack two PSRs were completely protected from challenge, with viremia and viral replication, pathology, and inflammation in the liver and spleen reduced to baseline. Therefore, PSRs are collectively indispensable for CCHFV infection and pathogenesis. We conclude that PSRs are not just cell entry factors but bona fide determinants of infection, dissemination, and disease by CCHFV and legitimate targets for the development of new antiviral countermeasures.

papers.title: Dietary tryptophan rescues growth impairment during giardiasis independently of parasite burden
papers.abstract: Giardiasis is an intestinal disease caused by the parasite Giardia duodenalis. Intestinal barrier dysfunction during Giardia infection has been linked to childhood growth stunting, particularly in communities with prevalent malnutrition and repeated exposure to Giardia. In pediatric cohort studies, growth stunting has been strongly associated with asymptomatic Giardia detection in fecal samples. Several studies have described potential mechanisms by which Giardia disrupts the epithelial barrier, but less is known about factors that may support epithelial homeostasis in response to infection. Microbiota-derived tryptophan metabolites that activate aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AHR) signaling are a key pathway involved in epithelial barrier homeostasis. We tested whether dietary tryptophan availability influenced host growth outcomes and aryl hydrocarbon receptor activity during giardiasis. We used established murine Giardia malnutrition models and compared host growth, a correlate of barrier dysfunction, with a tryptophan-supplemented diet group. Giardia-infected mice fed a low-protein diet failed to gain weight whereas infected mice fed an isocaloric regular protein diet gained weight similar to diet-matched controls. Tryptophan supplementation of the low-protein diet rescued this diet-dependent and infection-induced weight defect in C57BL/6J and BALB/c mice. This growth rescue was associated with increased intestinal Cyp1a1 expression, a canonical AHR target, but without a reduction in infection burden. Glycine supplementation, used as a non-essential amino acid control that is not expected to generate AHR ligands, did not produce the same effect, suggesting that the growth rescue observed with tryptophan supplementation was not due to general amino acid supplementation. Measurements of circulating tryptophan metabolites in plasma showed limited and inconsistent differences across experimental groups, which may suggest that the growth rescue phenotype may be dependent on local intestinal or mucosal AHR-associated signaling rather than an increase in circulating metabolites. Our findings show that dietary tryptophan availability shapes host growth outcomes during giardiasis. This may also be important as it highlights that host nutrition may be a key contributor to post-infection growth impairment in young children.

papers.title: Prevention of Klebsiella pneumoniae antibiotic resistance plasmid dissemination by prophylactic or simultaneous CRISPR-Cas9 treatment.
papers.abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is one of the most prevailing challenges of the 21st century, driven in part by pathogens such as Klebsiella pneumoniae which frequently disseminate plasmids carrying AMR genes within and across species. Mobile CRISPR-Cas9 tools can limit the spread of AMR plasmids through selective targeting but suffer efficacy issues when faced with ecological realism. Here, we assembled a simple three-strain community to assay the effectivity of mobile CRISPR-Cas9 in preventing dissemination of a clinical K. pneumoniae blaCTX-M-15 plasmid from its native host. We applied an Escherichia coli donor carrying a mobile CRISPR-Cas9 plasmid and entirely prevented transfer of the K. pneumoniae AMR plasmid into a focal, plasmid-free, E. coli recipient. Under experimental conditions favouring CRISPR-Cas9 plasmid transfer, AMR plasmid uptake was blocked regardless of whether the CRISPR-Cas9 plasmid spread prophylactically or simultaneously with the K. pneumoniae AMR plasmid. Our work shows that mobile CRISPR-Cas9 tools can overcome barriers to successfully prevent dissemination of AMR plasmids. Prophylactic application is not essential, and AMR plasmid transfer can even be suppressed when AMR plasmids spread simultaneously with mobile CRISPR-Cas9 tools.

papers.title: Volatile organic compounds of L. enzymogenes LEC suppress the growth of fungal and oomycete pathogens and modify the cell physiology of Rhizoctonia solani
papers.abstract: Lysobacter enzymogenes LEC is a plant disease-suppressive bacterium. To obtain a more comprehensive understanding of its biocontrol activity and to identify further potential application methods, we investigated the function of its volatile organic compounds (VOCs). VOC activity was assessed in vitro using split-plate assays with eight different fungal and oomycete isolates and in planta against Pseudoperonospora cubensis on cucumber plants. The volatilomes of LEC and the less active L. enzymogenes DSM2043 were analysed by GC-MS analyses. Further, the effects of VOCs on cell physiology of Rhizoctonia solani were analyzed by fluorescence and transmission electron microscopy. The strongest inhibition of LEC VOCs was observed for Phytophthora infestans (94%) and Phoma lingam (83%), while inhibitions were lower for Rhizoctonia solani (42%) and Alternaria spp. (24% and 29%) and not detectable for two Fusarium isolates. VOC exposure also significantly reduced downy mildew caused by P. cubensis on cucumber plants (39%), although this effect was locally restricted to the leaf directly above the VOC source. In R. solani, VOC exposure reduced nuclei abundance and increased lipid accumulation. GC MS analyses revealed distinct volatile profiles between LEC and L. enzymogenes DSM2043 and identified ketones, such as 2-dodecanone and undecanone as candidate bioactive compounds, which is in agreement with previous findings. Our results demonstrate broad-spectrum VOC-mediated biocontrol activity, and thereby provide a more comprehensive understanding of its biocontrol activity and highlight new ways for potential applications of LEC.

papers.title: Koala retrovirus dynamics in the Snowy Monaro, NSW
papers.abstract: Koala Retrovirus (KoRV) is in transition from exogenous virus to endogenous element and shows distinct profiles between northern and southern koala populations. Northern animals carry high proviral copy numbers of endogenous KoRV-A and a range of exogenous subtypes, while southern koalas instead generally only possess degraded and recombinant versions of the virus. In this study we investigated the KoRV profiles of koalas in the Snowy Monaro (SM) region of southern NSW, which is at the intersection between northern and southern populations. We found that SM koalas have lower KoRV loads and proviral copy numbers than koalas from other northern populations. Plasma RNA subtype profiles were very consistent between individuals with all animals having KoRV-A at low relative abundance and high proportions of subtypes D and L. This pattern of subtype profiles is unique compared to other populations studied and suggests that KoRV-D and/or L may be endogenous in southern NSW or that KoRV-A is effectively suppressed in koalas from the region. Despite these unique profiles, in agreement with findings from other regions, higher KoRV loads were associated with C. pecorum shedding. Further, KoRV loads were temporally stable with no consistent changes found over time in koalas in the wild or koalas rescued from burnt habitat after fire and brought in for rehabilitation. Further studies into the role KoRV plays in disease susceptibility in southern NSW and into the endogenization status of KoRV-D/L will provide important insights into this model of retroviral endogenization and guide koala conservation efforts in the region.

papers.title: A MultiOmics time-resolved systems map of gene regulation in Toxoplasma gondii
papers.abstract: Understanding how T. gondii builds an invasion-competent cell has been limited by its rapid, asynchronous division cycle, incomplete gene function annotation, and studies that have examined one regulator or complex at a time. Here, we placed acute perturbation of 21 transcriptional and epigenetic factors, promoter occupancy, chromatin accessibility, and molecular validation on a common single-cell clock. The resulting consensus map links the lytic-cycle programs to candidate activating and repressive inputs, organizes genes into 108 co-regulated communities, and nominates regulatory partnerships that would not have emerged from any single data type. The work bridges three longstanding gaps: it resolves perturbation responses in cell-cycle time, distinguishes promoter occupancy from perturbation-linked regulation, and turns a large multidimensional dataset into an experimentally navigable map. We indeed confirmed known factor interactions such as MORC/HDAC3 and recovered combinations such as the Cdc5/SNIP1 and DMAP1/EPL1 as coregulatory nodes (that in other systems have been described to cooperate). Furthermore, we discovered a novel apicomplexan specific combination of AAF1/AP2XI-5 that provides mechanistic insights of the unique AP2 transcription factor family.

papers.title: Correlation of Live Imaging and Fixed-Expansion Microscopy to study intracellular pathogens
papers.abstract: Expansion microscopy (ExM) enables high-resolution fluorescence imaging by physically enlarging biological samples, but its application to intracellular bacteria remains challenging. Here, we adapted the Ten-fold Robust Expansion Microscopy protocol to study host-pathogen interactions. Expansion of Burkholderia thailandensis-infected epithelial cells revealed previously unresolved membrane architectures associated with bacterial cell-to-cell dissemination. While host cells expanded approximately 9-fold, bacterial cells displayed incomplete and heterogeneous expansion. We found that fixation conditions strongly influence bacterial expansion, while presence of peptidoglycan partially limits expansion. To connect the membrane ultrastructures revealed by expansion with infection dynamics, we developed Live-to-Fixed Expansion microscopy (LiFEx), a workflow that correlates dynamic events observed by live-cell imaging with high-resolution cellular structures resolved by ExM. By correlating T6SS-5 assembly with subsequent high-resolution membrane architecture, LiFEx revealed membrane alterations developing within minutes following T6SS-5 assembly. Together, our approach enabled the investigation of dynamic host-pathogen interactions across complementary spatial and temporal scales.

papers.title: Tissue-specific transcriptomic responses to early Toxoplasma gondii infection in sheep during congenital toxoplasmosis
papers.abstract: Toxoplasma gondii is a widespread zoonotic pathogen of major One Health concern, capable of causing congenital toxoplasmosis in both humans and sheep. Despite its impact, early host-parasite molecular interactions during acute infection in pregnant hosts remain largely unexplored. In this study, we characterized the transcriptomic responses of key tissues involved in early infection (the small intestine, mesenteric lymph nodes, and placenta) in pregnant ewes experimentally infected with T. gondii strain TgShSp1. RNA-seq analysis revealed pronounced, tissue-specific transcriptional changes at 6 days post-infection (dpi), particularly in the mesenteric lymph nodes, characterized by activation of interferon- and cytokine-mediated immune pathways. In contrast, transcriptional responses at 3 dpi were limited, consistent with a silent phase of parasite dissemination. Despite the absence of detectable parasite DNA, placentomes showed modest interferon-associated responses and upregulation of DNA repair and cellular stress pathways. These changes coincided with marked suppression of cell-cycle progression and extracellular matrix remodeling alongside inhibition of angiogenesis and hypoxia pathways. Altogether, early disruption of placental vascular function and tissue remodeling may contribute to fetal loss. In summary, these findings provide new insights into early host responses to T. gondii infection in a pregnant host and identify molecular mechanisms that may predispose to early fetal death during ovine congenital toxoplasmosis.

papers.title: Chikungunya virus live-cell reporter systems reveal cell-type-dependent antiviral responses to ribavirin
papers.abstract: Chikungunya virus (CHIKV) remains a significant global public health threat, yet antiviral discovery is limited by experimental systems that provide little mechanistic resolution and rely heavily on transformed cell lines of uncertain physiological relevance. Here, we developed complementary live-cell CHIKV reporter systems comprising a dual-fluorescent subgenomic replicon and fluorescent infectious viruses that enable real-time monitoring of distinct stages of the viral replication cycle. By coupling an nsP3-tagged reporter to genomic RNA translation and replication with a subgenomic reporter of structural gene expression, we achieved temporal resolution of early and late replication events in living cells. Functional validation using replication-defective and subgenomic RNA-deficient mutants confirmed that the system distinguishes between viral RNA replication and downstream structural gene expression. Application of these reporters revealed distinct antiviral responses across transformed and physiologically relevant human cell models. Ribavirin and the nsP2 inhibitor RA-0002034 potently inhibited CHIKV replication in transformed cell lines. Unexpectedly, ribavirin activity was markedly diminished in primary human skeletal muscle myoblasts and dermal fibroblasts, despite robust antiviral effects in commonly used screening cell lines. Mechanistic studies showed that ribavirin-mediated inhibition was rescued by guanosine but not inosine supplementation and was recapitulated by mycophenolic acid, consistent with guanine nucleotide depletion as the predominant antiviral mechanism under the conditions tested. Notably, inhibition through this pathway was substantially less effective in primary human cells. Together, these findings establish versatile live-cell CHIKV reporter systems for mechanistic studies of viral replication and reveal striking cell-type-dependent differences in response to guanine nucleotide depletion. Our results demonstrate that host-cell context can profoundly influence both CHIKV replication and antiviral susceptibility, highlighting the importance of physiologically relevant models for understanding virus-host interactions and antiviral mechanism.

papers.title: Toward closing a heartwater monitoring gap with a new pan-species ELISA suitable for domestic ruminants, wildlife, and camels.
papers.abstract: Heartwater, caused by the tick-borne bacterium Ehrlichia ruminantium, threatens ruminant production in sub-Saharan Africa and the Caribbean. Serological surveillance relies on species-specific ELISAs, so wildlife and camelids, which are potential reservoirs or sentinels, have no validated tools. We developed and evaluated a pan-species indirect ELISA prototype (ID Screen Ehrlichia ruminantium Indirect Multi-species, Innovative Diagnostics) that detects anti-MAP1-B antibodies in all mammals. A positivity threshold of 30% relative positivity percentage (RPP) was empirically established from 707 heartwater-negative cattle, goat and sheep sera from three regions (maximum RPP 22.1%). Against a goat-specific reference ELISA (n = 503), the prototype showed 98.2% sensitivity, 97.2% specificity and 97.6% overall agreement. ROC analysis identified a Youden-optimal cut-off of 29.96%, confirming the empirical threshold. Inter-assay reproducibility was satisfactory (mean CV 7.4%), and qualitative classification remained stable across runs, including for a near-threshold sample. In four vaccinated sheep, the prototype detected seroconversion at the same time points as a sheep-specific ELISA. In non-domestic hosts, the assay gave uniformly low RPP values in 24 zoo animals of ten species from a heartwater-free area. By contrast, 4.5% of 111 dromedary camels from Chad exceeded the threshold. Eight wildlife species from Kruger National Park (n = 405) were tested and five species presented high median RPP values. This single-protocol assay provides a reproducible tool for integrated heartwater surveillance across livestock, camelids and wildlife, in Africa, in the Caribbean and in all countries threatened by the emergence of heartwater.

papers.title: Degree bias predicts, outperforms and improves machine learning phage-host interaction predictions
papers.abstract: Machine learning (ML) models predicting phage-host interactions are widely used to prioritize phages for phage therapy. The Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic (AUROC) metric is standard for model evaluation, with reported high scores (0.7 - 0.95) suggesting strong predictive power. However, because phage-bacterium networks are highly structured, these scores can be inflated by "degree bias", the baseline likelihood of infection driven purely by average phage infectivity and bacterial susceptibility. Here, we show that an interaction-naive model based solely on network degrees achieves higher global AUROC scores than five published ML models across ten datasets, indicating that global AUROC primarily reflects network structure rather than predicted interactions. Using randomized degree-conserved networks and degree-stratified evaluation, we isolate true interaction predictions and demonstrate that current ML model performance is far more modest than global AUROC suggests. Finally, we demonstrate that regressing out degree bias from training data improves interaction predictability and boosts global and stratified performance. Our work provides a critical framework for model evaluation and a straightforward route to improve ML-guided phage selection.

papers.title: Integrative multi-omics decoding of the host response to Klebsiella pneumoniae infection reveals an itaconate-centred metabolic-immune axis and a spatially organised inflammatory programme
papers.abstract: Background: Klebsiella pneumoniae (Kp) is a leading cause of hospital and community acquired pneumonia and bacteraemia, and hypervirulent and carbapenem resistant lineages continue to expand worldwide. Although individual omics layers of Kp infection have been profiled, the host-level molecular logic that connects transcriptional, cellular, metabolic and spatial programmes has not been systematically integrated. Methods: We curated 16 public datasets spanning four modalities-bulk and dual host pathogen RNA-seq (six datasets; 118 libraries), single-cell RNA-seq (four datasets; {approx}164,000 cells), untargeted/targeted metabolomics (four datasets; 1,842 molecular features) and Visium spatial transcriptomics (two datasets; {approx}11,400 spots) covering murine lung infection models, hypervirulent and classical Kp strains, carbapenem-resistant isolates and human clinical specimens. Datasets were harmonised through a standardised pipeline (Salmon/DESeq2; Scanpy/Harmony; MetaboAnalyst; RCTD/spacexr), and integrated by WGCNA, GSVA, CellChat, Monocle3, SCENIC, joint-pathway analysis, RCTD deconvolution, and machine-learning feature selection (LASSO, random forest, SVM-RFE, XGBoost) with 1,000x bootstrap internal validation and independent external validation. Results: Kp infection evoked a coherent 920 gene neutrophil inflammatory response ({approx}520 up-/{approx}400 down-regulated genes) dominated by IL-17/TNF/NF-{kappa}B signalling, neutrophil degranulation, HIF-1-linked glycolysis and itaconate biosynthesis. A turquoise co-expression module (r = 0.86 with infection status) yielded a ten-gene hub signature (IRG1, S100A9, IL1B, CXCL2, SLC7A11, HMOX1, PTGS2, NFKBIA, LST1, FCGR3B). Single-cell profiling resolved twelve major lung lineages and eleven myeloid substates, tracing a Monocle3 trajectory from Cxcr2hi inflammatory neutrophils through an Irg1/Slc7a11hi oxidative phase into Cxcr4hi/Trem2hi suppressive states; CellChat identified S100A8/A9-TLR4 and CXCL2-CXCR2 as the most amplified axes (8.5x and 4.2x). Metabolomics revealed 30-fold pulmonary itaconate accumulation together with succinate and lactate elevation, glucose/glutamine depletion and glutathione collapse, and joint-pathway analysis positioned the TCA-cycle itaconate and ferroptosis modules as the strongest convergent perturbations. Spatial transcriptomics mapped these programmes onto five anatomical niches, with IRG1 expression peaking in the infection core (58% neutrophil content) and declining radially. A ten-gene host-response classification model reached AUC=0.958 in discovery, 0.937 in internal validation and 0.884-0.912 in two independent external cohorts (Brier score 0.071). Conclusions: By vertically integrating public multi-omics data, we define an itaconate-centred metabolic-immune axis that couples inflammatory myeloid expansion to spatially segregated metabolic niches, and we deliver a validated host-side molecular signature that discriminates Kp infection from non-infected states.

papers.title: Abundance-weighted analysis and deep functional metagenomic selection reveals unrecognized diversity of soil-derived streptothricin acetyltransferases
papers.abstract: Streptothricins (STCs) are broad-spectrum antibiotics under investigation for their therapeutic potential against antibiotic-resistant Gram-negative pathogens. However, the extent and diversity of genes that confer resistance to STCs, or their environmental resistome, remains largely unknown and is essentially limited to a handful of STC acetyltransferases. Here, we used a deep functional metagenomic approach to uncover previously unrecognized STC resistance determinants. A functional metagenomic library containing ca. 700 Gigabases of soil metagenomic DNA was selected for resistance to nourseothricin (NTC), a mixture of STC congeners, resulting in collection and sequencing of nearly 30,000 resistant clones. An abundance-weighted sequence analysis identified 265 acetyltransferase-like candidates spanning broad phylogenetic, taxonomic, and genomic diversity. Re-cloning and experimental testing of 18 candidates chosen to cover acetyltransferase sequence space confirmed that 10 conferred significant NTC resistance in Escherichia coli. Phylogenetic analyses identified three previously uncharacterized STC acetyltransferase lineages, designated as SatC, SatD, and SatE. Despite substantial sequence divergence from characterized streptothricin acetyltransferases (maximum amino acid identities of approximately 31% for SatC and SatD and up to 47.5% for SatE), these enzymes largely retained key residues associated with streptothricin binding and catalysis. In addition to strongly increasing NTC resistance, expression of the SatC construct in E. coli also significantly decreased susceptibility to the aminoglycoside antibiotics amikacin and kanamycin. Together, these findings reveal a substantially broader than previously known environmental repertoire of STC acetyltransferases and demonstrate how deep functional metagenomic selections, combined with abundance-weighted hit calling, phylogenetic analysis, and structural prediction, can uncover novel resistance functions.

papers.title: A droplet-to-data workflow for antimicrobial screening of complex matrices
papers.abstract: Screening plant extracts and other complex natural matrices for antibacterial activity is complicated by optical interference and population averaging in conventional bulk assays. Droplet-based assays mitigate interference while enabling high-throughput assessment of bacterial subpopulations. However, analyzing the resulting image data involves difficult image processing, classification, and interpretation. Here, we present a democratized workflow for antimicrobial screening in complex matrices that combines a polydisperse droplet-based assay with EasyFlow 2.0 (EF2), our updated droplet image analysis platform. EF2 offers stable containerized deployment, expanded polydisperse droplet support, automated thresholding and MIC estimation, LLM-assisted data exploration, and import of other software outputs such as CellProfiler (CP) measurements and CellProfiler Analyst (CPA) classification models. As proof of concept, we applied this workflow to assess the antibacterial and aggregation-modulating effects of chemically distinct extracts of Taraxacum officinale, Rhodiola rosea, and Lonicera caerulea against Escherichia coli. Extracts were chemically characterized by HPLC-MS and evaluated using both standard 96-well plate microdilution and droplet-based assays. In total, 27,059 droplets were segmented in CP, classified into four growth phenotypes using a CPA random forest model, and analyzed in EF2. The droplet-based assay reached minimal inhibitory concentration (MIC) at lower extract concentrations than 96-well plate microdilution and revealed extract-specific aggregation effects: L. caerulea reduced E. coli aggregation, whereas T. officinale did not. R. rosea reduced growth in the 96-well plate microdilution assay, but high concentrations caused droplet gelation that prevented droplet-based analysis, showing that sample components must be checked for compatibility with droplet formation. These results illustrate that the EF2-centered workflow supports rapid, automated MIC estimation through unsupervised thresholding when labels are unavailable, and four-class aggregation phenotyping when a CPA model is supplied. This workflow offers flexible, scalable screening, potentially extendable beyond plant extracts to other complex sample matrices.

papers.title: The influence of drug dosing regimen on extinction and adaptation during experimental evolution in Candida albicans
papers.abstract: The antifungal azole drug fluconazole (FLC) is frequently prescribed for treating Candida albicans infections. Azole drugs are typically fungistatic; they inhibit cell growth rather than kill susceptible cells within a population. Therefore, fungal populations can adapt to fluconazole through increased drug resistance or increased drug tolerance (the ability of a subpopulation of susceptible cells to grow slowly at inhibitory drug concentrations). To our knowledge, no prior experiments have examined how different factors influence extinction propensity, although previous in vitro studies show that both drug concentration and strain background can influence adaptation. To determine how the drug dosing regimen, namely fluconazole concentration and transfer duration (i.e., the amount of time between transfer into fresh medium), influenced extinction and adaptation in Candida albicans, we conducted a fully factorial series of short in vitro evolution experiments. Dosing regimen significantly influenced extinction: all replicates evolved at all drug concentrations survived the 48 h and 72 h transfer experiments, yet the extinction rate increased sharply from low to high drug concentration with 24 h transfers. Increases in drug tolerance were frequent regardless of the dosing regimen. In contrast, drug resistance and growth rate both tended to decrease following evolution at higher drug concentrations. Fluconazole-evolved replicates exhibited frequent increases in cross-tolerance and decreases in cross-resistance in a panel of other azole drugs. Genome size changes were common in some strain backgrounds evolved to higher fluconazole concentrations, regardless of transfer times. Combined, our results indicate that many experimental factors can influence the trajectory of adaptation, and show that extinction in a fungistatic drug occurs readily at high drug concentrations with rapid transfers.

papers.title: Genomic Potential vs. Pathogenic Reality: Functional Virulence Variation in Pseudomonas aeruginosa
papers.abstract: Despite the rapid expansion of bacterial genome sequencing, predicting pathogen virulence from genomic information remains a major challenge. To study this association, we integrate comparative genomics, functional phenotyping, host-pathogen interaction assays, and infection outcomes across a diverse collection of 28 Pseudomonas aeruginosa isolates, representing clinically relevant diversity in serotype, type IV pilus group, and flagellar type. While virulence-associated systems were broadly retained across the strain collection, isolates displayed substantial variation in phenotypic behavior and pathogenicity. Genotypic classifications based on pilus, flagellar, siderophore, or secretion system characteristics were poor predictors of virulence-associated phenotypes. Pathogenicity in a Galleria mellonella model varied markedly among strains and was most strongly associated with surface-associated motility, whereas other virulence traits and quorum-sensing genotypes showed limited predictive value. In a three-dimensional lung epithelial cell model, inflammatory responses were negatively correlated with activity of the type III secretion system effector ExoS, suggesting a role in modulation of host immune signaling. Together, these findings demonstrate that virulence emerges from functional deployment of conserved virulence repertoires, rather than their mere presence. By linking genomic diversity to phenotypic expression, pathogenicity, and host responses within a single strain collection, this study highlights fundamental limitations of gene-content-based virulence prediction and underscores the importance of integrating genomic and functional data to better understand P. aeruginosa virulence.

papers.title: Complementing Biosafety Levels With Societal Safety Levels
papers.abstract: Biosafety level (BSL) classifications of biological agents have succeeded at minimizing occupational risk inside laboratories, but largely neglect the potential for onward transmission. As a result, many non-transmissible pathogens that could kill at most one individual per person exposed require greater containment than 1918 influenza, a virus that killed 50-100 million and might cause a new pandemic today. Laboratory workers are consenting professionals; the public is not. We recommend complementing BSLs with explicit thresholds for expected societal harm. Here we formalize Societal Safety Levels (SSLs) based on expected public fatalities per year, which we quantify from (i) estimated probability of laboratory release, (ii) likelihood of societal transmission, and (iii) consequence. SSLs would apply specifically to laboratory research with replication-competent potential pandemic pathogens, and would not restrict field surveillance, sequencing, or countermeasure development using non-replicating systems or pandemic-incapable agents. We find that applying the 0.1 expected deaths per facility-year standard common across multiple major-hazard industries to potential pandemic pathogen research would require marked safety improvements. Complementing BSLs with SSLs would establish enforceable accident-safety thresholds for pandemic-capable pathogens, bringing high-risk biological research into alignment with the quantitative safety standards that help other hazardous industries operate with public acceptance.

papers.title: Mechanistic insights into coronavirus inhibition by a distinct base-modified adenosine analog targeting the viral polymerase
papers.abstract: Nucleoside analog (NA) inhibitors of viral polymerases are a chemically diverse and prominent class of antivirals, with most agents bearing sugar modifications to induce chain termination. Compounds with a modified base yet natural ribose are comparatively rare and typically incorporated to act as virus mutagens, raising significant safety concerns. How nucleobase modifications interfere with polymerization and the molecular basis of this effect remain poorly understood. We here define the mechanism of 6-ethyl-modified 7-deazaadenosine (EDA), a recently identified coronavirus (CoV) inhibitor that does not induce virus mutagenesis. Its strong activity spans across multiple CoVs and cell models and is dictated by the 6-ethyl substituent, with poor tolerance for smaller, larger or heteroatom-containing substituents. At the level of SARS-CoV-2 RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp), EDA-triphosphate incorporates as a mimic of ATP but not other NTPs, inducing immediate stalling but also excision by the viral 3'-to-5' exonuclease. While EDA incorporation prevents extension with a second EDA residue, the stalling of natural NTP incorporation is transient and still allows the formation of longer products. A similar phenomenon is observed with template-embedded EDA. Cryo-EM analysis with SARS-CoV-2 RdRp revealed that 3'-terminal EDA is accommodated without distortion of the template:primer duplex, but its 6-ethyl group induces rearrangements in the NTP binding pocket that prevent stable binding of the incoming nucleotide. The mechanistic findings were validated through antiviral studies with SARS-CoV-2 mutants bearing core substitutions in the RdRp or exonuclease. Together, these findings position EDA as a mechanistically distinct base-modified NA prototype that has relevance beyond coronaviruses and underscores the ever-expanding versatility of NA-based polymerase inhibitors.
